chunks.heading: What is electric charge?
chunks.body: Charge is a property of matter that can be positive, negative, or neutral. Most objects are neutral because their positive and negative charges balance out.

chunks.heading: Where charge lives in an atom
chunks.body: Protons in the nucleus carry positive charge, and electrons around them carry negative charge. Electrons are much easier to move than protons.
chunks.checkText: Which particle is easier to move: protons or electrons?

chunks.heading: Gaining or losing electrons
chunks.body: An object becomes charged when it loses or gains [[phys-protons-electrons|electrons]]. Losing electrons gives it a positive net charge, and gaining electrons gives it a negative net charge.

chunks.heading: Measuring charge: the coulomb
chunks.body: The coulomb (C) is the standard unit for measuring [[phys-charge-basics|charge]]. A single electron carries a tiny charge of about -1.6 × 10^-19 C.
chunks.checkText: What is the SI unit for electric charge?

chunks.heading: Conductors let charge move, insulators don't
chunks.body: In conductors, such as metals, electrons move freely between atoms. In insulators, such as plastic or glass, electrons are held tightly and cannot move easily.

chunks.body: Charged objects push or pull on each other with an electrostatic force. Objects with the same charge repel, and objects with opposite charges attract.

chunks.heading: What is an electric field?
chunks.body: An electric field is the region of space around a charged object where another charged object would feel a force. Every charged object has one.

chunks.heading: Drawing electric field lines
chunks.body: Field lines show the direction and shape of an [[phys-electric-field|electric field]]. They point away from positive charges and towards negative charges.

chunks.heading: How close lines show field strength
chunks.body: Where [[phys-field-lines|field lines]] are packed close together, the electric field is strong. Where they spread apart, the field is weaker.

chunks.heading: Force on a charge in a field
chunks.body: A charge placed in an [[phys-electric-field|electric field]] feels a force given by F = qE, where q is its charge and E is the field strength.

chunks.body: Moving a charge within an [[phys-electric-field|electric field]] can store or release energy, just like lifting a ball stores gravitational energy. This stored energy is called electrical potential energy.

chunks.body: Potential difference (V) is the energy given to each unit of charge as it moves between two points. It is measured in volts.

chunks.body: Coulomb's law says the force between two point charges grows with the size of the charges, but shrinks fast as the distance between them grows. Doubling the distance cuts the force to a quarter.

chunks.body: The strength of the [[phys-electric-field|electric field]] around a single point charge gets weaker the further away you move, following the same pattern as [[phys-coulombs-law|Coulomb's law]].

chunks.heading: What is electric current?
chunks.body: Electric current is the flow of electric charge, usually carried by moving electrons in a wire. It is measured in amperes (A).

chunks.heading: A circuit needs a closed loop
chunks.body: Current only flows when a circuit forms a complete, closed loop from one terminal of a power supply to the other. A break anywhere stops the flow.

chunks.body: Conventional current is defined as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a battery. Real electrons actually flow the opposite way, negative to positive.

chunks.body: An ammeter measures [[phys-current|current]] and is connected in series, meaning it sits directly along the same path the current flows through.

chunks.heading: How a battery powers a circuit
chunks.body: A battery stores chemical energy and transforms it into electrical potential energy. This energy pushes electrons around a circuit, giving them the energy to keep moving.

chunks.body: Resistance measures how hard it is for [[phys-current|current]] to flow through a material. Conductors have low resistance, while insulators have high resistance.

chunks.body: Ohm's law says that for many conductors, potential difference equals current multiplied by [[phys-resistance|resistance]]: V = IR. If resistance stays constant, doubling the voltage doubles the current.

chunks.body: Ohmic conductors, like most resistors, have a constant resistance and give a straight-line graph of current against voltage. Non-ohmic conductors, like light bulbs, have a resistance that changes.

chunks.body: Kirchhoff's voltage law says the potential differences around any closed loop of a circuit must add up to zero. Energy gained from the battery equals energy lost in the components.

chunks.body: Kirchhoff's current law says the total current flowing into a junction must equal the total current flowing out. Charge is never created or destroyed in a circuit.

chunks.heading: Why homes use parallel wiring
chunks.body: Household circuits use [[phys-resistors-parallel|parallel]] wiring so every appliance gets the full voltage and can be switched on or off without affecting the others.

chunks.body: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. If you cut a magnet in half, you just get two smaller magnets, each still with both poles.

chunks.heading: Materials that magnetise easily
chunks.body: Iron, cobalt and nickel are called ferromagnetic materials because they become magnetised much more easily than other materials.

chunks.heading: Magnetic domains inside a material
chunks.body: A [[phys-ferromagnetic|ferromagnetic]] material is made of tiny regions called magnetic domains. In an unmagnetised material, these domains point in random directions and cancel each other out.

chunks.heading: How a material becomes magnetised
chunks.body: Placing a [[phys-ferromagnetic|ferromagnetic]] material in an external magnetic field lines up its [[phys-magnetic-domains|magnetic domains]] in the same direction, turning it into a magnet.

chunks.body: A magnetic field is the region of space around a magnet where a magnetic force can be felt. Field lines run from the north pole to the south pole.
